[h2]Resumen del Juego[/h2]
The Labyrinth of Grisaia es una aventura casual disfrazada de “solo leer un ratito” y de repente ya son las 3 a.m. y estás cuestionando tus decisiones de vida. Es una novela visual con estética anime, romance y drama, donde el verdadero laberinto no es el título… es tu estabilidad emocional cuando la historia decide ponerse seria (y luego recordar que también tiene contenido adulto).

La propuesta es simple: sentarte, avanzar texto, tomar decisiones (cuando te dejan) y dejar que la trama haga su magia. No esperes “jugabilidad” en el sentido tradicional: aquí el gameplay es tu paciencia, tu curiosidad y tu tolerancia a que el tono pase de adorable a violento como si nada. Primera impresión: producción cuidada, vibra intensa y la clase de narrativa que te agarra del cuello con una sonrisa.

[h2]Lo Adorable y lo Turbio (como el propio juego)[/h2]

Lo Bueno:
✅ 📖 Buena trama con drama y romance que sí saben pegar donde duele  
✅ 🎵 Gran banda sonora: acompaña perfecto los cambios de humor y tensión  
✅ 🎨 Estilo 2D anime sólido y consistente, ideal para novela visual  
✅ ☁️ Steam Cloud: para que tu “solo un capítulo más” se sincronice en todos lados  
✅ 😈 Se atreve a mezclar tonos (adulto/violento/adorable) sin pedir permiso

Lo No Tan Bueno:
❌ 🏆 0 logros: Steam te mira y dice “¿y tu dopamina de checklist, campeón?”  
❌ 🎮 “Aventura, Casual” = mucho texto y poca interacción; si buscas acción, aquí no es  
❌ 🧍 Un jugador y actualmente 1 jugador activo: la soledad también es parte del lore  
❌ 🔥 Contenido sexual y desnudos: no es “gratis”, pero sí puede sentirse invasivo si no vas mentalizado  
❌ ♻️ Al ser secuela/continuación, no siempre se siente amigable si llegas sin contexto previo

The Labyrinth of Grisaia serves as the bridge between the introductory character-focused drama of The Fruit of Grisaia and the series’ grander, more ambitious narrative arcs. Developed by Frontwing and published by Frontwing USA, it expands the universe in two principal directions: first, by offering “after stories” that show what life looks like for each heroine after the events of their respective routes; and second, by finally pulling back the curtain on protagonist Yūji Kazami’s past in a lengthy, emotionally charged main storyline. Where the first game focused on healing the heroines’ trauma, The Labyrinth of Grisaia turns inward and exposes the wounds Yūji has spent a lifetime concealing. This tonal shift gives the sequel a broader emotional spectrum—alternating between warm domestic epilogues and stark depictions of survival, violence, and psychological strain.

The after stories are the most immediately accessible part of the game, offering fans a chance to revisit the heroines and see how their lives evolve in the safety of Mihama Academy. These segments range from sweet and romantic to comedic and fan-service-heavy, often leaning into slice-of-life comfort rather than deep drama. They expand on the bonds built in the first game, showing glimpses of happiness and closure after the intense, trauma-driven character arcs. While some stories lean more heavily on humor or indulgence than narrative weight, they deliver exactly what returning players expect: warm epilogues, extra characterization, and a sense that each girl’s emotional journey has continued beyond the final scenes of Fruit of Grisaia. Even if uneven in tone, they offer a rewarding emotional cooldown and an affectionate nod to the fans who invested in each route.

The true centerpiece of The Labyrinth of Grisaia, however, is the Grand Route, known as The Cocoon of Caprice. This storyline shifts the spotlight entirely onto Yūji and serves as the first comprehensive exploration of who he is beneath the calm, stoic exterior. Through a series of flashbacks, confessions, and tense revelations, the game traces his childhood, his fraught relationship with his family, his training, and the shadowy forces that turned him into a deadly operative. It is a harsh, unflinching portrayal that reframes Yūji not as a mysterious helper figure, but as someone who has been shaped by unimaginable pressure and loss. The writing here is darker, more grounded, and more somber than anything in the first game, painting a portrait of a young man molded by circumstance and survival rather than choice. For many players, this route is the emotional core of the entire trilogy, adding context that elevates both past and future events.

Visually and stylistically, the sequel maintains the polished presentation expected from Frontwing. Character sprites remain expressive and clean, CG illustrations are vivid and impactful, and the overall production quality enhances both the lighthearted comedy and the grimmer dramatic moments. The soundtrack plays an equally important role, switching between warm, playful tunes for the after stories and heavier, more atmospheric tracks during the main route. The transition between tones is often dramatic, and while this can occasionally feel abrupt, the audiovisual design ensures that each emotional beat lands with the intended weight.

Despite its many strengths, The Labyrinth of Grisaia is not immune to flaws. The tonal contrast between the after stories and the Grand Route can be sharp, creating an uneven emotional rhythm. The writing in the lighter segments can feel looser or more comedic than necessary, occasionally undercutting the emotional depth established in the first game. Meanwhile, the Grand Route’s heavy subject matter—depictions of psychological trauma, child exploitation, and moral ambiguity—can feel overwhelming, even brutal, for players expecting a more balanced narrative. This inconsistency in tone and intensity can make the overall structure feel fragmented, as if two very different visual novels were packaged together under one title.

In terms of gameplay structure, the sequel is more linear than its predecessor. With no major branching choices and minimal replay variation outside of revisiting the after stories, the game focuses more on narrative expansion than player agency. For some, this streamlined approach is welcome, as it emphasizes character backstory and continuity; for others, the lack of route diversity may limit long-term engagement. Once the after stories and Grand Route are completed, there is little mechanical incentive to return beyond revisiting favorite scenes.

Ultimately, The Labyrinth of Grisaia succeeds as a middle chapter that deepens the universe, enriches its characters, and sets the stage for the trilogy’s final act. It gives fans what they most want: closure for the heroines, revelations about Yūji, and a more complete understanding of the forces shaping the overarching narrative. While its structure and tone may feel uneven, its emotional impact is undeniable, and its willingness to explore darker, more mature themes enhances the gravity of the world it builds. For players invested in the Grisaia series, this installment is an essential and rewarding chapter—one that turns the focus inward, challenges expectations, and prepares the narrative for its larger culmination in The Eden of Grisaia.

Rating: 8/10

The new characters like Yuuji’s old friends in particular are just pieces of cardboard compared to the Mihama’s five. And while the big villain’s introduction is pretty effective, the supernatural elements that already start to creep up around him look unnecessary and out of place.

If you’re dead set on continuing to Rakuen, then I guess the backstory part is still worth a read, but certainly not otherwise.

This will be a continuation of my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/hifumi-chan/recommended/345610/]review of the Fruit[/url] and it will be about the full version of the game, not the Steam one, since I hadn't played through this version aside from re-reading the Yumiko After.

[b]Warning, there could be some spoilers below![/b]

The Labyrinth, or Grisaia no Meikyuu - the romanized name is more familiar to me - is the second game in the main Grisaia trilogy. You can say that it's a sort of a mix between a fandisk and a sequel for the Fruit, since it consists of two parts: the After stories for all five girls and the main story for Yuuji. Also there is a bunch of short anecdotic stories which is basically an expansion for the Fruit's common route, and (in the original Japanese release) Dave's hentai corner with several H-scenes for other characters (some of them are [b]really[/b] questionable both here and in Eden).

All five of the After stories are just a very sweet stories with the events (not so) shortly after the end of the girls' routes in Fruit. Though, Sachi's After is a very... unique type of story, as well as Makina's. I can understand why people complain here about Makina's story, since she actually have very little time in it outside the nonexistent H-scenes in the Steam release. This is a fun expansion for those who want to look at their favourite girls one more time. As well as any fandisk for any VN out there.

The main story of the Grand route (The Cocoon of Caprice) in Labyrinth has some issues. It does a great, an awesome job in explaining Yuuji's past and introducing Kusakabe Asako to us, but... the scenario writers lost it. [i]A little.[/i] First, the story takes place one year after the events of the Fruit's common route. Everyone's particular issues had been resolved in a mystical way and every one of the girls thanks Yuuji for this. If you remember the events of the Fruit's routes, this will raise a GIANT question for you, since almost no one here have problems which could be resolved so easily in a span of a year. But OK, let's say it's a completely alternate timeline where the girls also for some reason partially knew about each other's past.

Yeah, the timeline. The main part of the story is the discussion about the Yuuji's autobiography found by Sachi, presented as one big flashback with several short interludes. And there is the main problem of the story itself. It is not consistent in regards to the characters' actual age and it tries to jam too many events in a period of time which is too small. We know for a fact from Amane's route in the Fruit that the [spoiler]Takizono bus incident[/spoiler] took place in September 2005. Now it's summer in 2012 (in Fruit the date was presented mainly as 20XX, but here it's clear now) and we can easily calculate Amane's age - she is 19, about to be 20 (at one point she even mentioned it herself). That makes the other ones being somewhere between 17 and 19, which is also correct, in relation to Sachi's route - her past in partially linked to Amane's. But if we follow the events of the flashback very closely, we will find out that these events cover at least 8 years of Yuuji's life, starting from [spoiler]losing his sister[/spoiler]. If you are not an avid fan of Grisaia like me, you'll probably shrug it off, but for me it was something like a bad splinter stuck in my thumb. =) Aside from that, the flashback really does a good job at building the character, even if some events look outright fictional in terms of common sense. The latter is tolerable here, but it takes a leap for the worse in Eden, though, by making the story pretty close to the second-league Hollywood blockbuster.

But holy cow, I still love it. And I want to make it to the Asako's hut in the forest one more time. Forget my whines, just choose which version you want to buy and play it.

For me, "Labyrinth" is the undisputed highlight of the Grisaia trilogy. Whilst others may (fairly) criticize it for its perceived lack of content when compared to its predecessor, I personally feel it offers a much more consistent experience, which is, in part, due to the shorter game length.

It's also in (no small) part due to the main arcs focus on some of the more interesting characters & relationships, especally Yuuji, JB, & Asako. Also, unlike "Fruit", all five of the side stories in Grisasia are pretty enjoyable, but in return, none of them are particularly special, either - They're just low investment/low reward slice of life fillers, which works for me, as I believe both "Fruit" & "Eden" have serious issues when it comes to getting the most out of their emotional plot ideas...

The art is just as consistent as the first game, but the OST doesn't feel anywhere near fresh enough, seeing how most of it is taken straight from "Fruit". The opening/ending songs, however, are very good indeed. Technically, the game still has one of the most frustratingly useless auto modes known to man, but at least this one has cloud saving.

I guess whether or not you'll prefer this game to the titles it's sandwiched between will come down to preference, but if you, like myself, found Yuuji & JB more interesting than all of the sidekicks, & want to learn a little bit about what got them to where they are today, then the main arc of Labyrinth is definitely worth 10-15 hours of your time.

[h1]PLEASE NOTE THAT I PLAYED A NON-STEAM VERSION OF THE LABYRINTH OF GRISAIA UNRATED OFF DENPASOFT.COM FOR THE SAME PRICE AS STEAM. I PLAYED 20-30 HOURS ON THIS GAME![/h1]

Okay, now that wonderful experience is out of the way, let’s get into the game, shall we?

[h1]What is there to offer? What is the game content?[/h1]

The Labyrinth of Grisaia is the second installment of the Grisaia series right after the previous game, The Fruit of Grisaia, and definitely has some important/fun things to do in it. Not only do you get small, but interesting after stories to all the endings in the previous game, you also get Yuiji’s entire past explained, which is the bulk of this game. Unfortunately, this game doesn’t offer any choices or decisions like in the first game but gives you hours of cool content. You also get a Short Story section which is just 30 mini-stories that have no relevance to the plot whatsoever. And lastly, you get a, no joke here, a Masturbation Station which is just an erotic group of stories/fantasies that I’m sure the fan base wanted in the game so Front Wing made it. But I’m not joking; it’s literally called a Masturbation Station! It’s around 4 sex stories with random characters from the series.

[h1]Is the game worth it?[/h1]

When it actually comes to the game itself, I wouldn’t mark it at a face value of $30.00, that’s just too much for truly nothing text. I know the first game does have a lot of Slice of Life moments with no relevance to the actual plot whatsoever, but unlike The Fruit of Grisaia, Labyrinth doesn’t seem to have that drive for you to actually read those little sections for the enjoyment of reading it. I just remember reading The Fruit of Grisaia for hours without getting bored but I just didn’t get the same feeling for Labyrinth. Nevertheless, the game was very entertaining. But when it comes down to it, you have two choices: 

1)	YOU EITHER WATCH THE ANIME AND MISS OUT ON THE EXTRA CONTENT WITH THE ENDING SCENES

2)	BUY THE GAME FOR FULL-PRICE OFF DENPASOFT.COM AND PLAY THE GAME

No matter what you’re thinking of, it really comes down to this. I’ve watched both the anime and the visual novel, and they are literally the exact same thing. You get some extra scenes that the anime didn’t have in the visual novel, but for $30.00, it may seem better to spend it on other stuff. But if you’re thinking about buying the game, PLEASE just buy the unrated version off Denpasoft. I can’t stress this enough considering that a good portion of this game is literal H-scenes which Steam cuts in this version

[h1]Overall…[/h1]

So overall, I would recommend this game even though it may seem that I don’t in the review. I really love this show/series, and I personally found this installation very enjoyable and worth the money after finishing it. And even though I spent closer to 50+ hours on The Fruit of Grisaia, this game was fun. Just don’t expect to have choices or anything like the first and have alternate endings. This game is for Yuiji’s past and that’s all. The extra stuff is just filler so that the user doesn’t feel entirely ripped off for spending that much money on this. I can’t wait for the 3rd one to be released Unrated, and I can’t wait to see what Front Wing has in store for us!

Labyrinth of Grisaia is the second game in the series, and completing the original is most definitely a requirement before starting this one. The setup is a little different here, with the game split into essentially three sections. 

First comes the epilogues of all the good endings from the first game- these are quite enjoyable and give a good deal of closure to those scenarios. Next up is the main route, Cocoon of Caprice, which tells the painful story of Yuuji's youth and past in the form of flashbacks, along with reactions from characters in the present time learning the information. Finally there is a series of amusing short stories set in all different time periods and being just for fun. 

There are no major changes from the original game, and it's a very smooth continuation. This is a shorter entry and there are no dialogue options this time around, you simply choose your scenario from the main menu. Be warned that this ends on a cliffhanger for the final game in the trilogy, Eden of Grisaia. 

It may not have all the magic of the original but if you enjoyed Fruit of Grisaia, this is basically required reading. Enjoy.
